title: Observer lifecycle and incident runloop for LLM serving
author: Alex Chen
content:
Overview

Purpose: This document defines the end-to-end observer lifecycle and incident runloop for Redwood's model-serving surface (hosted API, Dedicated, Private), and bundles runbooks, postmortem expectations, on-call rotation guidance, game day templates, and status/ customer communication examples. It is intended for on-call engineers, SREs, support, and product owners.

Scope: model-serving API endpoints, inference runtime clusters, KV/prefix caching, routing/fallback policies, and the components that directly impact inference SLOs (p95 latency, error-rate, availability). This doc does NOT cover: billing incidents, non-inference control plane failures, or infra provider outages (those are covered under eng-sre/runbooks).

Quick links:
- Runbook: High-latency model-serving cluster (below)
- Postmortem template (section: Postmortem & RCA)
- Status templates (section: Status & customer comms)

1) Roles and responsibilities

- Primary on-call (Responder): first investigator and owner of the incident until carrier handoff. Responsible for initial triage, mitigation, and comms.
- Bridge operator (if invoked): runs the incident bridge, coordinates stakeholders, and keeps a public running summary.
- Escalation on-call (Area owner): team-level escalation for service-specific fixes (e.g., runtime, routing, infra).
- SRE incident lead: validates mitigations, authorizes wider mitigations (e.g., autoscaler changes, capacity swaps).
- Customer-facing comms (Support / CS): drafts and publishes customer messages using the status templates.

2) Severity classification and SLO thresholds

We use a simple three-tier severity system for model-serving incidents. Severity should be assigned during triage and visible on the incident ticket and status page.

Severity | Definition | Target response | Escalation window
---------|------------|-----------------|-------------------
P1       | Large-scale outage: >25% of production requests affected OR p95 latency >5x SLO for >5 min | Acknowledge within 2 min | Escalate to SRE & product within 10 min
P2       | Partial outage / customer impact: single region or class degraded, p95 latency 2–5x SLO | Acknowledge within 15 min | Escalate within 60 min if unresolved
P3       | Localized or performance regression with mitigation available; no major customer disruption | Acknowledge within 2 hours | Triage in next business day

SLOs (example):
- p95 latency: 250 ms (hosted small models)
- error-rate: <0.2% (5xx + timeouts measured at API edge)
- availability: 99.95% monthly

3) Incident lifecycle and runloop (step-by-step)

1. Signal and detection
   - Alerts originate from metrics (Prometheus), tracing anomalies (Jaeger), and customer reports. Priority to signals that touch p95 and error-rate.
   - Initial evidence to capture: top-5 alert graphs, time window, affected regions, model(s), recent deploys, and increase in queue depth.

2. Acknowledge & declare
   - Primary on-call acknowledges the alert in the paging system within the severity window.
   - If P1/P2, stand up incident bridge (Zoom/Google Meet) and create the incident ticket in Jira/Status (template).

3. Triage (first 10 min)
   - Determine blast radius: region(s), customer subsets, models, routing tiers.
   - Check recent deploys: Git commit, rollout ID. If deployment <15 minutes prior, suspect rollout.
   - Check autoscaling events, GPU preemption events, and queue backlog.

4. Mitigate (minutes -> hours)
   - Preferred mitigations: graceful fallback to compatible model variant, reduce QPS via routing policy, enable prefix cache, increase concurrency on affected nodes, or scale reserve pool.
   - If mitigation applied, verify p95 and error-rate returning toward SLO.

5. Stabilize & communicate
   - Once p95 within acceptable range or a durable mitigation is in place, move to ‘stabilize’. Post an initial status update: summary, impact, next steps, ETA for mitigation, and owner.

6. Recovery & post-incident work
   - After service is stable for the confirmation window (30–60 minutes), close the incident with a remediation plan and schedule a postmortem.

4) Decision ladders & escalation matrix (cheat-sheet)

- If p95 > 2x SLO for >10 min AND error-rate increasing: escalate to SRE incident lead.
- If queue depth > 10x baseline and tail latency rises: trigger capacity augmentation (add reserved nodes) and notify infra.
- If rollout suspected: immediately pause rollout and roll back if safe.

5) Runbook: High-latency model-serving cluster (operational run steps)

Scope: used by on-call for cross-region high p95 or persistent tail latency.

Immediate checklist (order matters):
1. Collect evidence (commands/queries):
   - kubectl get pods -n runtime -l app=model-serving -o wide
   - prometheus query: rate(request_duration_seconds_bucket[5m]) and topk(10, increase(request_errors_total[5m]))
   - curl -sS "https://observability.internal/api/top-traces?service=model-serving&window=5m"
2. Check recent rollouts:
   - deployctl history runtime/model-serving --since 30m
3. Inspect node resources:
   - nvidia-smi (on affected nodes)
   - kubectl describe pod <pod> | egrep -i "OOM|Evicted|Preempt"
4. Apply quick mitigations:
   - Toggle runtime-routing to fallback pool: curl -X POST https://controlplane.internal/route/update -d '{"policy":"fallback","target_pool":"reserve"}'
   - Increase concurrency for model-serving: k8s patch deployment runtime/model-serving -p '{"spec":{"template":{"spec":{"containers":[{"name":"inference","env":[{"name":"MAX_CONCURRENCY","value":"64"}]}}]}}}'
5. Verify: run synthetic load for the affected model variant (locally or from staging runner) and measure p95.

Important metrics to include in the incident ticket:
- p95, p50, p99 latency for affected model(s)
- API 5xx & 429 counts (edge and runtime)
- Queue depth and average queue time
- CPU/GPU utilization by node pool

6) Runbook: Capacity exhaustion and noisy neighbor containment

Symptoms: increasing queue length, marginal requests failing with timeouts, noisy processes consuming GPU memory.

Steps:
1. Identify noisy pod(s): kubectl top pod --all-namespaces --containers | sort -r -k3
2. Throttle noisy customers via routing tags: controlplane route throttle --tag customer:cust-123 --rate 10rps
3. Spin up reserved nodes (if autoscale not available): terraform apply -var='reserved_pool=3' -target=module.gpu_pool
4. Schedule controlled eviction for confirmed memory leaks (drain node and cordon).

7) Postmortem & RCA process (requirements and template)

Timeline requirements:
- Postmortem draft due: within 72 hours of incident stabilization for P1/P2; within 14 days for P3.
- Action items assigned with owners and deadlines within the postmortem.
- Severity re-evaluation: PM and SRE must agree on severity and external communications.

Postmortem template (use as checklist):
- Title (concise)
- Incident ID, Severity, Start/End timestamps
- Summary: 2–3 sentence impact statement
- Timeline: minute-level timeline for first 60 minutes, then hourly
- Root cause: contributing factors, single root cause statement
- Corrective actions: short-term mitigations + long-term fixes (owner + due date)
- Follow-up: automation, test coverage, monitoring additions, runbook updates
- Customer impact and communications log (include status page and support tickets)

8) On-call rotations, handoffs, and tooling

Rotation policy (recommended):
- Primary rotation cadence: 1-week primary, 1-week secondary (shadow), then 2 weeks off.
- Handoff window: 30-minute overlap between shifts for verbal handoff and ticket review.
- Coverage for holidays: distributed on-call with explicit backup; team lead must approve changes 1 week in advance.

Handoff checklist:
- Review open incidents and priority tickets
- Check ‘health check’ dashboard: tail latency, error-rate, queue backlog, GPU pool utilization, status-page open incidents
- Confirm calendar availability and Slack contact info

On-call tooling quick commands:
- Acknowledge page: pagerctl ack <alert-id>
- Open incident ticket: incidentctl create --service model-serving --severity P1 --summary "<short>"
- Mute noisy alert rule: alertctl mute --rule <rule-name> --expires 15m (document reason)

9) Game day playbook (quarterly exercise template)

Goals: validate runbooks, test capacity augment workflows, exercise customer comms and incident bridge procedures.

Duration: 4 hours (wall time)
Participants: at least 2 on-call engineers, 1 SRE incident lead, 1 product lead, 1 support rep

Scenarios (pick 2 per game day):
- Sudden p95 spike in US-West after a model rollout
- Reserve pool exhausted with queuing in Dedicated customers
- Cache invalidation leading to mass cold starts and tail latency increase

Game day checklist:
1. Pre-brief: scope and inject points, safety checklist (no real customer traffic will be impacted—use staging or canary traffic).
2. Inject: simulated traffic pattern or toggle a feature flag to emulate failure.
3. Observe: measure detection time, triage time, mitigation time.
4. Review: collect timings, update runbooks, publish a 1-page after-action note.

10) Status page & customer communication templates

Status page principles:
- Be timely, factual, and concise.
- Use three updates: Acknowledged, Mitigating, Resolved.
- Include impact scope, affected models/regions, workaround, ETA if known, and owner contact.

Status page examples (short):
- Acknowledged (first post):
  Title: Elevated inference latency impacting hosted API (US-West)
  Body: We are investigating elevated p95 latency for text generation requests in US-West beginning at 2026-01-12T11:04Z. Impact: ~35% of requests experiencing elevated tail latency. Owner: Alex Chen. Next update: 11:20Z.

- Mitigating (follow-up):
  Title: Mitigation in progress — routing to reserve pool enabled
  Body: We have enabled fallback routing to a reserve node pool which has reduced the observed p95 by ~60%. We continue monitoring. Some customers on Dedicated may see brief increased queuing. ETA to stabilize: 30–45 minutes.

- Resolved:
  Title: Resolved — latency returned to expected levels
  Body: The fallback routing and a rollout pause resolved the incident. No further action required. We are scheduling a postmortem and will publish details within 72 hours.

Customer email template (for affected large customers):
Subject: Incident update — Inference latency (region US-West)
Body:
Hi <Customer name>,

We wanted to let you know we observed elevated inference latency starting at 2026-01-12T11:04Z affecting requests in US-West. Mitigation: we enabled fallback routing to our reserve pool and paused a recent rollout; service has returned to normal as of 2026-01-12T11:53Z.

Impact: Some requests may have experienced increased latency or transient errors. We do not believe customer data was affected.

Next steps: We will publish a postmortem within 72 hours with root cause and actions. If you would like direct support, reply to this message and we will open a support ticket.

— Redwood Inference Support

11) Runbook maintenance and governance

Owners and cadence:
- Each runbook must have an owner (engineer) listed and a quarterly review date.
- Postmortems trigger runbook updates when procedures changed.
- Game days validate runbook accuracy; failures to follow the runbook result in an action item assigned to the owner.

Checklist for runbook updates:
- Verify command outputs and locations (new APIs or endpoints)
- Confirm ACL/permission requirements are current
- Update mitigation scripts and test them in staging

Appendix: Useful commands and links
- Observability dashboard: https://observability.internal/d/model-serving
- Incident ticket template: incidentctl template --name model-serving
- Pager and on-call schedule: https://oncall.internal/teams/model-serving
- Example postmortem: /confluence/postmortems/2025-model-serving-p1-example

Contact: For questions or suggested changes, ping #eng-oncall or assign a doc change request to Alex Chen.
